Angola.summary: Angola is thought to be a potentially important route for the spread of herders, farmers and livestock into southern Africa, yet a 2018 survey of the evidence found hardly any archaeology from the region. Pottery from a shell midden at Benfica, on the northern coast, has been proposed as a possible origin of the Kalundu pottery tradition. Little can be said specifically about 570-632.

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Benin.summary: No written records survive for this land in 570–632, and its communities are known only in the most general terms. The kingdoms later associated with the area, such as Allada, Abomey (Dahomey), Ouidah, Nikki and Porto-Novo, arose only between the 12th or 13th century and the 19th century. Across Africa, iron smelting, known since the first millennium BCE, was still spreading.

events.t: Iron and copper smelting, known in Africa since the first millennium BCE, continues to spread; by c. 1000 it is found across the continent.

sources.title: Benin (Britannica Students)
Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Botswana.polity: Foragers and herders; early iron-using farmers at Tsodilo
Botswana.summary: At the Tsodilo Hills in the north-west, with over 4,500 rock paintings and a long record of human occupation, the Early Iron Age village of Divuyu dates to the 6th-8th centuries; its people forged iron and worked copper into small ornaments. The nearby site of Nqoma dates to the 7th-10th centuries. No written records exist.

events.t: Divuyu at the Tsodilo Hills is occupied by iron- and copper-working people, dated to the 6th-8th centuries.

sources.title: Tsodilo
D. Miller, Iron age metal working at the Tsodilo Hills, Northwestern Botswana (PhD thesis, 1992)

Burkina Faso.summary: Iron production in the region was very old: Douroula, part of a UNESCO World Heritage property, dates back to the 8th century BCE. The property's other furnace sites show intensified production in the second millennium CE. Little is specifically dated to c. 570-632.

events.t: Iron smelting, attested at Douroula since the 8th century BCE, is long established; sites of this era are poorly dated.

sources.title: Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy Sites of Burkina Faso

Burundi.polity: Early Iron Age farming communities (Urewe culture and successors)
Burundi.summary: Burundi's Central Plateau, with good farming soils and easy access to iron ore and wood, was home to Early Iron Age communities of the Urewe culture. Radiocarbon dates suggest iron smelting began here early in the first millennium BCE at the latest and flourished until about the 7th century CE. No written sources exist, and the later kingdom of Burundi did not yet exist.

events.t: Iron smelting in the Rwanda–Burundi region, practised for over a millennium, reaches the end of its Early Iron Age flourishing (c. 7th century).

sources.title: P. Craddock, I. Freestone, A. Middleton and M.-C. Van Grunderbeek, 'Early Iron Age iron-smelting debris from Rwanda and Burundi, East Africa', Historical Metallurgy 41(1), 2007

Cameroon.polity: Farming and foraging communities (much reduced in the south)
Cameroon.summary: The border region of Nigeria and Cameroon is the homeland from which Bantu-speaking peoples spread. In southern Cameroon, radiocarbon evidence shows a population collapse c. 400-600 CE and very low activity for centuries after, reaching near-zero values about 900-1000 CE. Archaeology is the only evidence.

events.t: Southern Cameroon's forest communities are much reduced after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)

Central African Rep..summary: No written sources exist. Across the Congo rainforest to the south, radiocarbon evidence shows a widespread population collapse between c. 400 and 600 CE, followed by markedly low human activity until about 1000 CE; only 61 sites in the whole rainforest have well-dated evidence from 600-1000 CE.

events.t: In the Congo rainforest to the south, human activity is very low after a collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)

Congo.summary: Early Iron Age communities had expanded across the Congo rainforest, including the western Congo basin, but radiocarbon evidence shows a widespread population collapse c. 400-600 CE, followed by markedly low human activity until about 1000 CE, when new pottery groups and a second expansion phase appear.

events.t: After a rainforest-wide population collapse c. 400-600 CE, human activity stays low until about 1000 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)

Côte d'Ivoire.summary: No written records survive for this land in 570–632, and its peoples are known only in general terms. The states later found here came long afterwards: the Senufo founded the kingdom of Kong in the 11th century, and Akan and Anyi peoples migrated in and founded kingdoms much later still. Across Africa, iron smelting, known since the first millennium BCE, was still spreading.

events.t: Iron and copper smelting, known in Africa since the first millennium BCE, continues to spread; by c. 1000 it is found across the continent.

sources.title: Côte d'Ivoire (Britannica Students)
Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Dem. Rep. Congo.polity: Farming and foraging communities; Kamilambian iron-users in the Upemba
Dem. Rep. Congo.summary: Across the Congo rainforest, including the inner Congo basin, radiocarbon evidence shows a population collapse c. 400-600 CE and low activity until c. 1000. In the Upemba Depression in the south-east, the Kamilambian, the area's earliest ironworking culture (c. 6th-8th century), relied on farming and fishing and preceded the Kisalian, which began c. mid-8th century.

events.t: Kamilambian communities, the Upemba Depression's earliest ironworking culture (c. 6th-8th century), occupy sites such as Kamilamba and Sanga.

sources.title: Nicolas Nikis, Upemba Depression (The Encyclopedia of Ancient History, 2021)
sources.publisher: Wiley-Blackwell; author copy via Royal Museum for Central Africa

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)

Eq. Guinea.summary: The mainland lies within the Congo rainforest between southern Cameroon and Gabon, where radiocarbon studies show a population collapse c. 400-600 CE and very low human activity for centuries afterwards. No written sources exist.

events.t: Rainforest communities in the region are much reduced after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)

Gabon.summary: Iron working had reached Central Africa about 3,000 years ago, but radiocarbon evidence shows a sharp population collapse in Gabon c. 400-600 CE and very low human activity until about 1000 CE. Genetic data suggest that today's Bantu-speaking communities of Gabon arrived only in the second expansion phase (1000-1500 CE).

events.t: Gabon's forest is thinly occupied after a population collapse c. 400-600 CE; resettlement follows from about 1000.

sources.title: Seidensticker et al., Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion (Science Advances 7, 2021)
Central Africa: The Iron Age

Gambia.polity: Communities of the Senegambian megalithic zone
Gambia.summary: Along the Gambia River, communities raised circles of laterite pillars, quarried with iron tools, beside burial mounds, as at Wassu and Kerbatch. Excavated material from the sites suggests dates from the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE. Nothing is known of their rulers or languages from writing.

events.t: The Senegambian stone-circle tradition, spanning the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE, is in use at sites such as Wassu.

sources.title: Stone Circles of Senegambia

Ghana.polity: Farming communities (not the medieval Ghana empire)
Ghana.summary: Modern Ghana lies far from the medieval Ghana (Wagadu) empire, which was in southeastern Mauritania and Mali. In the Koma area of the north, stone-circle mounds with terracotta figurines were once dated to the 13th-19th centuries, but newer radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dates place occupation and mound building between the 6th and 10th centuries; they may have been shrines.

events.t: Koma Land mounds with terracotta figurines, possibly shrines, are being built in northern Ghana; dates span the 6th-10th centuries.

sources.title: Kankpeyeng & Nkumbaan, Ancient Shrines? New Insights on the Komaland Sites of Northern Ghana (2009)
Ghana (historical West African empire)

Guinea.summary: Iron-using farming communities lived in the upland savanna and forest zones of West Africa in this era. The great states of the region came centuries later. The period is known only through very limited archaeology.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities occupy the highlands and upper Niger; few sites are dated to this era.

sources.title: Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Guinea-Bissau.summary: The precolonial history of this coast has not been fully documented in the archaeological record, and no written sources exist for 570–632. Little can be said with confidence about its communities in this period. Across Africa, iron smelting, known since the first millennium BCE, was still spreading.

events.t: Iron and copper smelting, known in Africa since the first millennium BCE, continues to spread; by c. 1000 it is found across the continent.

sources.title: Guinea-Bissau: History
Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Lesotho.summary: The mountains were home to San hunter-gatherers. The caves and rock shelters of the Maloti-Drakensberg, including Sehlabathebe National Park in Lesotho, hold the largest and most concentrated group of rock paintings in Africa south of the Sahara, representing the spiritual life of the San, who lived in the area over 4,000 years. Evidence is archaeological and rock art.

sources.title: Maloti-Drakensberg Park

Liberia.summary: Almost nothing is known of this land in 570–632; no written records exist. The ancestors of most of Liberia's present indigenous peoples, such as the Kpelle, Bassa, Grebo, Kru and Mano, migrated here from the western Sudan only in the late Middle Ages, long after this period. Across Africa, iron smelting, known since the first millennium BCE, was still spreading.

events.t: Iron and copper smelting, known in Africa since the first millennium BCE, continues to spread; by c. 1000 it is found across the continent.

sources.title: Liberia (Britannica Students)
Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

Malawi.polity: BaTwa foragers and Iron Age farmers
Malawi.summary: BaTwa hunter-gatherers, present since the Late Stone Age, painted rock shelters such as those at Chongoni, the richest concentration of rock art in Central Africa. Farming peoples also made rock art there; the Chewa, whose ancestors lived in the area from the Iron Age, painted until the 20th century. Specific evidence for 570-632 is scarce.

sources.title: Chongoni Rock-Art Area

Namibia.summary: The drier western half of southern Africa, including Namibia, shows an enduring presence of herders with sheep and some cattle, ahead of and during the spread of farming. Directly dated sheep bones and pottery come from Leopard Cave, and other sites have yielded metal-working and metal artefacts, though their occupants are unclassified. Evidence is archaeological.

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Nigeria.polity: Farming communities and the early town of Ife; Nok culture long ended
Nigeria.summary: The Nok terracotta culture (c. 500 BCE–200 CE), one of Africa's earliest ironworking centres, had ended centuries before. Ife in the southwest, occupied since c. 350, was growing into an important urban centre in its Archaic period (to c. 800). Near Lake Chad, settlement mounds such as Daima record long-lived Iron Age farming villages. Igbo-Ukwu's famous copper-alloy castings date to about the 10th century, after this period.

events.t: Ife, in its Archaic period (to c. 800), develops as an important urban centre with sedentary farming and stone monoliths.

sources.title: Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
Nok Terracottas (500 B.C.–200 A.D.) (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)
Graham Connah, 'The Daima Sequence and the Prehistoric Chronology of the Lake Chad Region of Nigeria', Journal of African History

Rwanda.polity: Early Iron Age farming communities (Urewe culture and successors)
Rwanda.summary: Rwanda's Central Plateau, with good farming soils and easy access to iron ore and wood, was home to Early Iron Age communities of the Urewe culture. Iron smelting began here early in the first millennium BCE at the latest and flourished until about the 7th century CE. Non-Urewe Early Iron Age furnaces in the region date to about the 6th century. No written sources exist.

events.t: Early Iron Age iron smelting continues in the region; non-Urewe furnaces such as Kabuye II date to about the 6th century.

sources.title: P. Craddock, I. Freestone, A. Middleton and M.-C. Van Grunderbeek, 'Early Iron Age iron-smelting debris from Rwanda and Burundi, East Africa', Historical Metallurgy 41(1), 2007

Senegal.polity: Communities of the Senegambian megalithic zone
Senegal.summary: Communities in the Gambia river region raised circles of laterite pillars, quarried with iron tools, beside burial mounds, as at Sine Ngayene and Wanar. Excavated material suggests dates from the 3rd century BCE to the 16th century CE. No written sources describe them.

events.t: The Senegambian stone-circle tradition is in use at sites such as Sine Ngayene and Wanar.

sources.title: Stone Circles of Senegambia

Sierra Leone.summary: People had lived in what is now Sierra Leone for thousands of years, and the Bulom, Temne and Limba of the coast were probably its earliest inhabitants among present-day peoples. No written records exist for 570–632, and its communities in this period are known only in general terms. Across Africa, iron smelting, known since the first millennium BCE, was still spreading.

events.t: Iron and copper smelting, known in Africa since the first millennium BCE, continues to spread; by c. 1000 it is found across the continent.

sources.title: Sierra Leone (Britannica Kids)
Guinea Coast, 500–1000 A.D. (Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History)

South Africa.polity: Iron-using farmers in the east; herders and foragers in the west
South Africa.summary: Iron-using farmers, directly ancestral to the Bantu-speaking peoples who form South Africa's majority today, had arrived from about 200 CE. Their sites in the east show pottery, metal-working, cultivation and livestock. The Lydenburg Heads, the earliest sculpture found in southern Africa, date to c. 500-700 CE. Herders held an enduring presence in the drier west.

events.t: The Lydenburg Heads, terracotta heads found near Lydenburg, are made; they are dated c. 500-700 CE.

sources.title: South Africa: The Iron Age
Lydenburg heads
sources.publisher: University of Cape Town, Centre for Curating the Archive

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Togo.summary: In the Bassar region of the north, an iron production industry flourished from as early as the Early Iron Age; the large village of Dekpassanware worked iron through the Early and Later Iron Ages. Production grew rapidly in the Later Iron Age, feeding regional trade. Written sources do not exist, and much of the period is undated.

events.t: Bassar communities continue an iron-working tradition begun in the Early Iron Age; large-scale production comes later.

sources.title: de Barros et al., The early iron metallurgy of Bassar, Togo (Azania 55, 2020)

Uganda.polity: Iron-using farmers of the Great Lakes
Uganda.summary: Around Lake Victoria, farmers had used iron and made Urewe-tradition pottery for centuries. Larger centres such as Ntusi developed only after about 1000 CE. No written sources exist, and few sites are dated precisely to this era.

events.t: Iron-using farming communities, heirs of the Urewe tradition, occupy the Lake Victoria basin.

sources.title: David W. Phillipson, African Archaeology, 3rd ed. (2005)
Graham Connah, African Civilizations: An Archaeological Perspective, 3rd ed. (2016)

Zambia.polity: Early Iron Age farmers and foragers
Zambia.summary: Early farming in Zambia is attested by decorated pottery, though radiocarbon dating is often poor; rectangular hut floors are known from southern Zambia, and Kalambo Falls in the far north is among the recorded early sites. Pottery of ironworking groups in the Copperbelt and northern Zambia resembles that of the Kamilambian culture (c. 6th-8th century) of the Upemba. No written sources exist.

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)
Nicolas Nikis, Upemba Depression (The Encyclopedia of Ancient History, 2021)
sources.publisher: Wiley-Blackwell; author copy via Royal Museum for Central Africa

Zimbabwe.summary: Across the eastern half of southern Africa, early farmers left sites with pottery, metal-working, cultivation and livestock. In Zimbabwe, the granite shelters of the Matobo Hills, occupied from the Early Stone Age into historical times, hold an outstanding collection of rock paintings. Great Zimbabwe flourished only from the 11th to the 15th century. Evidence is archaeological.

sources.title: Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)
Matobo Hills
Great Zimbabwe

eSwatini.polity: Iron-using farmers and San foragers (poorly documented)
eSwatini.summary: Iron-using farmers, ancestors of South Africa's Bantu-speaking majority, had settled South Africa from about 200 CE, and decorated pottery and iron-working appear along the coast from southern Mozambique to KwaZulu-Natal. San hunter-gatherers lived in the nearby Drakensberg. No site in eSwatini itself is discussed in the sources consulted.

sources.title: South Africa: The Iron Age
Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)
